'''Robert Joseph Paton Williams''' (25 February 1926 – 21 March 2015<ref>{{cite journal |title=Obituaries |journal=University of Oxford Gazette |volume=145 |issue=5093 |date=23 April 2015 |page=499}}</ref>) was an English [[chemist]], an [[Emeritus]] [[Fellow]] at [[Wadham College, Oxford]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Williams|url=https://www.wadham.ox.ac.uk/people/emeritus-fellows/w/bob-williams|publisher=Wadham College, University of Oxford|access-date=23 March 2015|archive-date=3 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150503052105/https://www.wadham.ox.ac.uk/people/emeritus-fellows/w/bob-williams|url-status=dead}}</ref> and an Emeritus Professor at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="Thomson2015">{{cite journal|last1=Thomson|first1=Andrew J|title=Professor Robert JP Williams FRS (25/2/1926–21/3/2015)|journal=Journal of Biological Inorganic Chemistry|volume=20|issue=4|year=2015|pages=617–618|issn=0949-8257|doi=10.1007/s00775-015-1262-6|pmid=25913871|s2cid=39414172|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="MannThomson2015">{{cite journal|last1=Mann|first1=Stephen|last2=Thomson|first2=Andrew J.|title=Robert J. P. Williams (1926–2015)|journal=[[Angewandte Chemie]]|volume=127|issue=27|year=2015|pages=7856|issn=0044-8249|doi=10.1002/ange.201504131|bibcode=2015AngCh.127.7856M }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/news/rjpwilliams.html|title=R J P Williams (1926–2015)|publisher=University of Oxford|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160209102758/http://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/news/rjpwilliams.html|archive-date=9 February 2016|author=Anon|year=2015}}</ref><ref name=bio>{{History of Modern Biomedicine Research Group ID}}</ref>

==Education and early life==
Robert Joseph Paton Williams was born on 25 February 1926 in [[Wallasey]] to Ernest Ivor Williams, a customs and excise officer at [[Liverpool]], and Alice Williams (née Roberts), a milliner; he was the second of four children.

Williams failed to gain a scholarship to [[The Kingsway Academy|Wallasey Grammar School]], having missed six months’ schooling with [[diphtheria]], but his parents paid for him to attend. He went on to gain a place and be awarded a Postmastership<ref>''Postmastership'' is the term used at Merton College for what other colleges call a scholarship.</ref> to read chemistry at [[Merton College, Oxford]] in 1944. For his final undergraduate research year he worked with analytical chemist [[Harry Irving (chemist)|Harry Irving]]. This enabled him to establish an order of the relative stabilities of metal–organic complexes along the latter half of the [[Transition metal|transition series]] manganese through zinc.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Irving|first1=H|last2=Williams|first2=R J P|title=Order of Stability of Metal Complexes|journal=Nature|volume=162|issue=4123|pages=746–747|date=6 November 1948|doi=10.1038/162746a0|bibcode=1948Natur.162..746I|s2cid=6943144}}</ref> From these findings he saw a parallel with the selective uptake of metal ions by organisms.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Thomson|first=Andrew J|title=The science of RJP Williams|journal=Journal of Biological Inorganic Chemistry|volume=21|pages=1–3|date=2016|issue=1|doi=10.1007/s00775-015-1328-5|pmid=26759252|s2cid=18533741|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Williams’s plan was to continue working with Irving for his [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]], but he first visited the lab of [[Arne Tiselius]] at [[Uppsala University]]. He was impressed by what he saw there, and returned to Sweden after he gained his DPhil in 1950. During the longer stay he worked on protein purification and devised a method called [[High-performance liquid chromatography#Isocratic and gradient elution|gradient elution]] analysis.<ref name=rsbm>{{cite journal|last1=Hill|first1=H. A. O.|last2=Thomson|first2=A. J.|title=Robert Joseph Paton Williams MBE. 25 February 1926 – 21 March 2015|journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|year=2016|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2016.0020|volume=62|pages=541–570|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Williams then spent another period back at Merton, having won a junior [[research fellow]]ship, Then, “out of the blue, in 1954, [[Cyril Norman Hinshelwood|Cyril Hinshelwood]], then Oxford Professor of Chemistry, asked to see Bob.” He was told that three colleges—Christ Church, Pembroke and Wadham—needed a tutor in chemistry. “Each one will invite you to dine. Come back again in two weeks to give me your decision.”<ref name=rsbm/> Williams joined [[Wadham College, Oxford]] in 1955 and remained there for the rest of his life. His doctoral students include [[Peter Day (chemist)|Peter Day]],<ref name=daydhil/> [[Carole Perry]]<ref name=dphil/> and [[Michael Thor Pope]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1039/jr9590003442 | title = Distribution of molecular weights in some polyesters and polypeptides | journal = J. Chem. Soc. | pages = 3442–3446|last1 = Pope |first1 =M T |last2 =Weakley |first2 = T J  |last3 = Williams  | first3 = R J P| year = 1959 }}</ref>

William's work in pure inorganic chemistry led to a two-volume textbook of inorganic chemistry, written with Courtenay Phillips,<ref>{{cite book| title = Inorganic Chemistry: Principles and non-metals (volume 1)|author1=C. S. G. Phillips |author2=R. J. P. Williams |year = 1965|publisher= Oxford University Press|isbn = 978-0198551188}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| title = Inorganic Chemistry: Metals (volume 2)|author1=C. S. G. Phillips |author2=R. J. P. Williams |year = 1965|publisher= Oxford University Press}}</ref> He became increasingly interested in enzyme catalysis, and in particular the role of metal ions, as for example the role of copper in proteins.<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1007/s007750000146 | journal = J. Biol. Inorg. Chem. | last1 = Gray | first1 =H B | last2 = Malmström | first2 = B G |last3 = Williams  | first3 = R J P | volume = 5 | number = 5 | pages = 551–559 | title = Copper coordination in blue proteins| year = 2000 | pmid = 11085645 | s2cid = 1815405 }}</ref> He and [[Bert L. Vallee|Bert Vallee]] proposed of the concept of the [[entatic state]] whereby atoms and groups in enzyme active sites are maintained by binding to the apoenzyme in positions and states appropriate to catalyse reactions.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA | doi= 10.1073/pnas.59.2.498  | last1 = Vallee |first1 = B. L. |last2 = Williams| first2 = R. J. P. | title = Metalloenzymes: entatic nature of their active sites  | volume = 59 | number = 2 |  pages =  498–505 |year = 1968
| pmid= 5238980 | pmc= 224700 | bibcode= 1968PNAS...59..498V | doi-access= free }}</ref>

In the first paper ever published in the ''Journal of Theoretical Biology'' Williams argued that spatial separation of the H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>–</sup> ions produced in the conversion of ATP to ADP would be necessary for the catalysis.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = J. Theor. Biol. |doi= 10.1016/0022-5193(61)90023-6|title = Possible functions of chains of catalysts|last1 =Williams|first1 = R J P|volume = 1|number = 1|pages = 1–17|year = 1961|pmid= 13785509}}</ref> In the same year [[Peter D. Mitchell|Peter Mitchell]] proposed a similar idea in the form of the chemiosmotic hypothesis.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mitchell P | title = Coupling of phosphorylation to electron and hydrogen transfer by a chemi-osmotic type of mechanism | journal = Nature | volume = 191 | issue = 4784 | pages = 144–148 | date = July 1961 | pmid = 13771349 | doi = 10.1038/191144a0 | s2cid = 1784050 | bibcode = 1961Natur.191..144M }}</ref> In a special issue of the ''Journal of Theoretical Biology'' in celebration of 50 years of its existence Williams described the correspondence between Mitchell and himself.<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1016/j.jtbi.2010.09.021 | title = Chemical advances in evolution by and changes in use of space during time|volume= 268|number = 1| pages = 146–159|journal = J. Theor. Biol.|last1 =Williams|first1 = R J P|year = 2011| pmid = 20869970}}</ref>

Williams contributed to understanding of the distribution of the chemical elements in living organisms and in collaborationwith [[João J. R. Fraústo da Silva]] he wrote three books in this area,<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Fraústo da Silva|author-link=João J. R. Fraústo da Silva|first1=J J R|last2=Williams|first2=R J P|title=The Biological Chemistry of the Elements: the Inorganic Chemistry of Life|location=Oxford|publisher=Clarendon Press|isbn=0-19-850848-4|date=1991}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last2=Fraústo da Silva|first2=J J R|last1=Williams|first1=R J P|title=The Natural Selection of the Chemical Elements|location=Oxford|publisher=Clarendon Press|isbn=9780198558422|date=1996}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last2=Fraústo da Silva|first2=J J R|last1=Williams|first1=R J P|title=The Chemistry of Evolution: The Development of our Ecosystem|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=9780444521552|date=2005}}</ref> as well as a book with [[Rosalind Rickaby]]<ref>{{Cite book|last2=Rickaby|author2-link=Rosalind Rickaby|first2=R E M|last1=Williams|first1=R J P|title=Evolution's Destiny: Co-evolving Chemistry of the Environment and Life|location=Cambridge|publisher=RSC Publishing|date=2012}}
</ref> on geological aspects of life.

Williams retired in 1991 and devoted much of his retirement to the writing of the books mentioned.

===Awards and honours===
Williams was appointed [[Member of the Order of the British Empire]] (MBE) in the [[2010 New Year Honours]] for services to the community in North Oxford.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=59282 |date=31 December 2009 |page=23 |supp=y }}</ref>

He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1972|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1972]]<ref name=rsbm/> and was a Foreign Member of the Swedish, Portuguese, Czechoslovak and Belgian science academies. He was a medallist of the [[Biochemical Society]] (twice), the Royal Society (twice), the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (three times), the Federation of European Biochemical Societies (twice) and the International Union of Biochemistry.  He delivered the [[Bakerian Lecture]] in 1981 and won the [[Royal Medal]] in 1995.<ref name="Hasani Hoffmann 2015">{{cite web | last1=Hasani | first1=Ilire | last2=Hoffmann | first2=Robert | title=Academy of Europe: Williams Robert | website=Academy of Europe | date=21 March 2015 | url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Williams_Robert | access-date=10 September 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life==

While he was in Uppsala Williams met Jelly Klara Büchli, a Dutch  student from [[Groningen]]. They married in 1952 and then lived in Oxford. Jelly read English language and literature at [[St Hilda's College, Oxford]] between 1952 and 1955, but the birth of their first son, Timothy Ivor, interrupted her final exams. A second son, John M, was born in 1957. In 1981 Jelly published ''A Dutch Reader''.<ref>{{cite book|last=Williams|first=Jelly K|title=A Dutch Reader|publisher=[[Nelson Thornes]]|isbn=9780859503495|date=1981}}</ref>

Bob Williams died in the [[John Radcliffe Hospital]] on 21 March 2015.
